context: A processional cross from the Lasta region of Ethiopia, made of copper alloy in the early 15th century. Christianity has a very long history in Ethiopia, and crosses of many designs were made for use in church life. A processional cross is carried in a procession, usually mounted on a staff. The record lists it as 35.6 centimeters tall.

descriptions.k: This is a cross made of metal. It was made in Ethiopia a very long time ago, more than 500 years. A cross like this can be carried on a pole. What patterns can you find on it?
descriptions.g12: This metal cross was made in Ethiopia more than 600 years ago. It is a processional cross, which means people carried it in a parade or procession. Look at the patterns on it. Which lines curve, and which lines are straight? Can you find a pattern that repeats?
descriptions.g35: This copper-alloy cross was made in the Lasta region of Ethiopia in the early 1400s. It is a processional cross, which means it was carried in church processions, often on a staff. Ethiopian crosses are known for their detailed patterns and many different shapes. Look for repeated patterns and for places where there is open space. How does the maker turn a simple cross into a decorated work of art?
descriptions.g68: Ethiopia has one of the oldest Christian traditions in the world, and metalworkers there have made crosses in a great variety of shapes. This processional cross, made in the Lasta region in the early 15th century, would have been carried on a staff in church ceremonies. Its decoration, made in metal, shows how a sacred symbol can also be an object of craft. Notice how patterns, edges, and empty spaces work together. How does the design make you look closely at every part of the cross?
descriptions.g910: This early 15th-century processional cross from the Lasta region reflects Ethiopia's long Christian tradition and its metalworkers' skill at turning a single symbol into many forms. Ethiopian crosses vary widely by region and period, and decoration may include interlace, openwork, and repeated motifs. As a processional object, it was made to be carried and seen in motion, which affects how we think about its shape and surface. How do ornament and symbol balance on this cross, and how might its use in procession have shaped its design?
descriptions.g1112: Ethiopian crosses form one of the richest bodies of metalwork in Christian art, and this early 15th-century example from the Lasta region shows both the long continuity of the tradition and its regional variety. Its form, ornament, and size suggest an object designed for movement and display in church procession, but the museum record gives limited detail about its original context. Studying a cross like this raises questions about how art objects serve religion and craft at the same time, and about how a museum's setting changes the way a devotional object is seen. How can a viewer respect its original purpose while analyzing its design?

teacherNote.context: A copper-alloy processional cross from the Lasta region of Ethiopia, early 15th century. It is a religious object from the Ethiopian Orthodox tradition, so approach it with respect and focus on design and craft.
directions: Ask students to draw a simple cross and then add three kinds of repeated pattern, explaining their choices.
Discuss the difference between an object carried in motion and one displayed still, using this cross as an example.
Connect to geography: locate Ethiopia and the Lasta region on a map, and discuss the long history of Christianity in East Africa.
